idiom_name: memoized reader with defined? guard (ActiveRecord association proxy)
implementation_notes: Ruby defers inside an ordinary reader: '@author ||= gateway.find(@author_id)' runs the read on the first call and returns the cached value afterwards, with 'return @author if defined?(@author)' as the correct guard when nil or false are legitimate loaded values. The framework half is ActiveRecord: associations are proxies whose target is not loaded until needed - the first enumeration or attribute read issues the query and caches it - and includes/preload/eager_load are the prefetch escape hatch. What replaces the classic holder class is the reader method plus the association proxy, and the memoization itself is not synchronized.
code_sketch:
class Book
  def initialize(author_id, gateway) = (@author_id, @gateway = author_id, gateway)

  def author
    return @author if defined?(@author)      # nil is a loaded value
    @author = @gateway.find(@author_id)      # query on first call
  end
end
pitfalls: ||= re-runs the load whenever the result is false or nil; use defined? (or a loaded? flag) when absence is a legitimate value.
Memoization is not thread-safe: on JRuby/TruffleRuby - and on MRI when the loader blocks - two threads can both query, so a shared identity map is usually the better cache.
ActiveRecord caches the association per instance with no automatic invalidation, and rendering a collection without includes produces the classic N+1.
